network_thesis.headline: Korea's biggest micromobility fleet meets its fastest water fleet.
network_thesis.body: Korea is a peninsula wrapped in water — a megacity river (the Han), beach-and-bay metros (Busan), marquee islands (Jeju), a national marine park (Hallyeohaesang), and international corridors to Japan. Swing owns the street layer of that geography: the largest shared fleet of e-scooters, e-bikes and e-mopeds in the country, plus taxis in the same app. What Swing doesn't own yet is the water between its vehicles. A Navier foiling tier turns every pier into a Swing hub — ride a scooter to the water, fly across it, ride a scooter away on the far side.

stats.sub: scooters, bikes, mopeds & taxis in one app

network_thesis.how_to_read: Each card is a real, ready market. Start with Busan — the most renderable, ready pilot — or pick any cluster. Seoul / the Han River is the strategic hero. The phased sequence is our recommended path, not the only one.
network_thesis.coverage_note: The same Navier fleet that anchors our 4 proposed markets extends across Swing's full operating footprint of 4 water-relevant markets — each inheriting cities, corridors, and economics directly from the shared corridor registry.

partner_context.their_ambition: You are Swing — Korea's largest micromobility platform. You built the country's densest shared fleet of e-scooters, e-bikes and e-mopeds across 70+ cities, added taxis to the same app, launched the SWING+ membership, and expanded into Japan. You win by owning more of the short urban trip than anyone else.
partner_context.their_pressure: Street micromobility is contested, regulated and margin-thin. The next leg of growth comes from higher-value trips per member — and Korea's geography holds an entire trip class no micromobility player can serve: the water crossing. Seoul's 2025 Hangang Bus launch under-delivered on speed, Busan's bay has no in-app tier, and Jeju's islet ferries are aging.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: Navier is the missing middle leg of the Swing journey. A software-defined foiling fleet, booked in the Swing app, premium-priced, on the Han River, Busan's bay, Jeju's islets and the Hallyeohaesang marine park — with Swing scooters and bikes waiting at both piers. Nobody else can chain street and water this tightly.

hero.title: Swing × Navier — street to water, one app
hero.subtitle: Swing owns Korea's street layer. The water between its cities is the surface no one owns yet.
hero.what_we_do_together: We launch a Swing-booked foiling water tier across Korea's busiest water surfaces — the Han River, Busan's bay, Jeju's islets and the Hallyeohaesang marine park. Navier brings the software-defined hydrofoiling fleet and the network playbook now proven in the Maldives; Swing brings millions of members, the SWING+ subscription rails, and vehicles at every pier for the first and last 800 meters. Together we make the scooter-boat-scooter journey a single tap.

why_now: Foiling lifts the hull clear of the water: faster, dramatically more efficient per passenger-mile, smooth and near-silent, hybrid-capable with no charging dependency, and autonomy-ready. A ~100-vessel network is already ramping in the Maldives, and Korea's water is wide open — Seoul's 2025 Hangang Bus launch was criticised as too slow, Busan's waterfront has no in-app tier, and Jeju's islet ferries are aging. The operator that already parks a vehicle at every pier is the natural one to claim it.

why_navier_now.step_change: Hydrofoiling lifts the hull clear of the water, so a Navier vessel flies instead of plowing through chop - roughly 10x more efficient than a conventional planing boat, faster (30+ kt cruise), and dramatically smoother and quieter. It's software-defined and autonomy-ready, so the same fleet keeps getting better and cheaper to run over time.
why_navier_now.no_new_infrastructure: Navier rides on infrastructure that already exists - the Han River piers, Busan's harbour, Jeju's ports and the marine-park terminals. Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal; the Quanta-LR hybrid needs no charging infrastructure at all for the cross-border legs.
why_navier_now.the_moment: Three forces converge in Swing's backyard: the technology crossed from prototype to platform; a ~100-vessel network is ramping in the Maldives; and Korea's water surfaces — a slow new river bus, an un-monetized Busan bay, aging Jeju ferries — are ready to be switched onto a clean foiling tier that plugs straight into the app with a vehicle already waiting at both ends.

multimodal_fit: Swing already runs dense multimodal operations: tens of thousands of shared vehicles, live fleet rebalancing, in-app payments, membership pricing and taxi dispatch. A foiling water tier slots straight in — same app, same wallet, captain-partners alongside the street fleet, and a Swing scooter or e-bike staged at each pier so the water leg is door-to-door by default.

differentiation.why_navier: Software-defined and autonomy-ready — the same operations-first instincts Swing built its street fleet on. A ~100-vessel at-scale network already proving the model in the Maldives, directly relevant to Korea's many-island, river-and-coast geography. And uniquely with Swing: the only partner that can guarantee the first and last 800 meters of every water journey.

proof_points.claim: Swing is Korea's largest micromobility platform.
proof_points.evidence: The largest shared e-scooter / e-bike / e-moped fleet in Korea — tens of thousands of vehicles across 70+ cities — plus taxis in the same app and the SWING+ membership.

proof_points.claim: Swing is the consolidation winner in Korean micromobility.
proof_points.evidence: Profitable while peers retrenched, backed by a $24M Series B, expanded into Japan in 2022, and monetizing multimodal usage through subscription membership.

proof_points.claim: Korea's regulators are pulling marine fleets toward clean propulsion.
proof_points.evidence: Korea's national 'Toward Green Shipping by 2050' plan / 2030 Greenship-K strategy mandates eco-friendly conversion of public vessels and targets ~118 eco-friendly ships converted by 2030 on the path to net-zero domestic shipping by 2050 — a direct tailwind for a clean foiling tier.
proof_points.source: Korea Ministry of Oceans & Fisheries / Argus Media, 2023

proof_points.claim: Seoul's own river-transport push proves Han River demand — and the speed gap Navier fills.
proof_points.evidence: Seoul's ₩150B (~$105M) Hangang Bus launched in September 2025 and passed 300,000 cumulative riders within months, but drew divided reviews and was widely criticised as too slow to be real transport — exactly the fast-foiling-tier opening.
proof_points.source: Korea Times / Korea Herald / Straits Times, 2025–2026

objections.concern: Is the range enough across Korea's water?
objections.response: Korea's water splits cleanly into short hops and long line-hauls. The Han River commute (~11 nm), Busan's bay (~4 nm), Jeju's islets (~4–6 nm) and the Hallyeohaesang marine park (~12–30 nm) all sit well inside the Pioneer II / N35 70 nm all-electric envelope; the Busan↔Fukuoka (~110 nm) and Jeju↔Busan (~157 nm) line-hauls run on the Quanta-LR hybrid (700 nm, no charging infrastructure required).

objections.concern: Why succeed on the Han River where the Hangang Bus underwhelmed?
objections.response: The river bus is a slow conventional craft criticised as not-real-transport; a 30+ kt foiling tier is a different product entirely — a genuine cross-city commute, premium-priced and on demand in the the Swing app app Seoulites already use.

objections.concern: Korea's winters, monsoon and typhoon season cut operating days.
objections.response: Foils ride above the chop and software-defined routing flexes with conditions, so the fleet runs smooth on days conventional ferries cancel; demand concentrates in the long beach-and-islet seasons the fleet is sized for, while the cross-border and business line-hauls carry year-round flow.

objections.concern: Is the network model proven enough to commit to?
objections.response: A ~100-vessel, $100M, 3-year network is already ramping with JIH Global in the Maldives, and a second island-network anchor is signed with the WorldBridge Group in Cambodia — the same software-defined, autonomy-ready foiling model, directly relevant to Korea's river, coast and many-island geography.

phases.narrative: Busan is the proof market: a scenic beach-and-bay shoreline with no in-app water tier. A small Pioneer II / N35 fleet on the Haeundae–Gwangalli–Marine City hops and the Geoje run shows the Swing app users a water layer that feels like the rest of the app.

phases.label: Phase 2 — Jeju + the cross-border line-haul
phases.rationale: Layer in Korea's marquee island-tourism market (Jeju islet hops + resort arrivals) and the marquee international corridor (Busan↔Fukuoka) the Quanta-LR hybrid was built for.
phases.narrative: Jeju turns the story to premium leisure — all-weather islet hops and resort arrivals — while the Busan↔Fukuoka Quanta-LR line-haul opens the cross-border flow inside an app travellers on both sides hold.

phases.label: Phase 3 — the south-coast marine park + the Han River
phases.rationale: Carry the network into the Hallyeohaesang marine-park island-hopping mesh and the Jeju↔mainland line-haul, and stand up the strategic Han River commute once the Seoul map node is built.
phases.narrative: The south coast is where the island mesh matters — Yeosu, Tongyeong and their marine-park islands — and the Han River is the strategic hero: a fast foiling commute that turns Seoul's slow river bus into real transport.

phases.label: Phase 4 — the whole Korean water map
phases.rationale: With the clusters proven, knit them into one national in-app water tier across Korea's coasts, river and cross-border corridors.
phases.narrative: The end state: Swing's foiling water tier across the Han River, Busan's bay, Jeju, the Hallyeohaesang marine park and the cross-border corridors to Japan — one app, Korea's water.

Today the offshore islands run on aging ferries; there is no premium in-app foiling tier across the coast or the mainland line-haul. This is a high-spend leisure water market for the Swing app.

end_state.headline: The water layer of Korea's street-mobility champion — coast, river and islands, nationwide.
end_state.addressable_footprint: Every Korean water surface Swing already serves on land — the Han River through 10M-person Seoul, Busan's beach-and-bay metro, Jeju's island-tourism coast, and the Hallyeohaesang marine park.

steady_state.tam_framing: Jeju alone drew ~13.9M visitors in 2025, Seoul is a 10M-person megacity, and the Korea–Japan strait carries year-round business and tourism flow — all running today on slow river buses and aging ferries, a premium water-mobility surface no app has monetised.

end_state.narrative: Steady state is not a pilot count — it is the whole Korean water map. Busan proves the model, then Jeju and the cross-border line-haul, the Hallyeohaesang marine park, and the strategic Han River: 410 foiling vessels across four clusters, on 20+ corridors, booked entirely inside the Swing app — Pioneer II / N35 for the river, bay and islet capillaries and Quanta-LR for the long Jeju and Japan legs. The Maldives' ~100-vessel network is the unit; Korea is that model brought home to a peninsula wrapped in water — the water layer of the app Koreans already live in.
